items.title: Hypotheses
items.body: \(H_0\) (null hypothesis): assumed true. \(H_1\) (alternative): what we test for. One-tailed or two-tailed test.

items.title: Test Statistic
items.body: \(Z=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\sim N(0,1)\) under \(H_0\). Compare with critical value \(z_\alpha\).

items.title: Critical Region
items.body: Range of test statistic that leads to rejection of \(H_0\). For two-tailed 5%: |Z|>1.96. One-tailed 5%: Z>1.645 or Z<-1.645.

items.title: p-value
items.body: Probability of observing a result as extreme as the sample, assuming \(H_0\). Reject \(H_0\) if p\text{-value}<\alpha.

items.title: Type I and II Errors
items.body: Type I: reject \(H_0\) when true (probability = significance level \(\alpha\)). Type II: fail to reject \(H_0\) when false (probability \(\beta\)).

items.title: Testing Poisson/Binomial
items.body: Find \(P(X\geq x_0)\) (or \(P(X\leq x_0)\)) under \(H_0\). If <\alpha, reject \(H_0\). State conclusion in context.

body.en:
Steps: (1) State \(H_0\) and \(H_1\). (2) Specify significance level \(\alpha\). (3) Identify test statistic and its distribution under \(H_0\). (4) Find the critical region or \(p\)-value. (5) Compare and conclude in context.
One-tailed: H_1:\mu>\mu_0 or \mu<\mu_0. Two-tailed: \(H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0\) (split \(\alpha\) equally). Type I error: reject \(H_0\) when it is true (probability = \(\alpha\)). Type II error: fail to reject \(H_0\) when it is false.

Probabilistic Normalization & Moment Structure: Every probability model is governed by total probability conservation: \(\sum_x P(X=x) = 1\) for discrete random variables and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\) (with \(f(x) \ge 0\)) for continuous density functions. Expected value \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) acts as a linear operator (\(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]\)), whereas variance scales quadratically and adds for independent variables: \(\operatorname{Var}(aX \pm bY) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Hypothesis Testing)

body.en:
Why Variance Scales as \(a^2\) and Independent Variances Always Add: By definition, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mu_Y)^2]\). For \(Y = aX - bW\) with independent \(X, W\), subtracting its mean \(\mu_Y = a\mu_X - b\mu_W\) gives:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(a(X - \mu_X) - b(W - \mu_W))^2\right] = a^2\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)^2] - 2ab\,\operatorname{Cov}(X,W) + b^2\mathbb{E}[(W-\mu_W)^2] \]

Because independence implies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, W) = 0\), the cross term vanishes and \((-b)^2 = +b^2\), proving \(\operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(W)\). Uncertainty compounds whether random variables are added or subtracted.

Bags of flour are labelled 500 g. A sample of 25 bags gives \(\bar{x}=497\) g. Population SD is 8 g. Test at 5% whether there is evidence that bags are underweight.

\(H_0:\mu=500\), H_1:\mu<500 (one-tailed). \(Z=\dfrac{497-500}{8/5}=\dfrac{-3}{1.6}=-1.875\). Critical value: \(-1.645\). Since -1.875<-1.645, reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at 5% that bags are underweight.

Road accidents used to occur at a rate of 4 per week. After safety measures, only 1 accident is observed in one week. Test at 5% whether the rate has decreased.

\(H_0:\lambda=4\), H_1:\lambda<4. \(P(X\leq1)=e^{-4}(1+4)=5e^{-4}\approx0.0916\). Since 0.0916>0.05, do not reject \(H_0\). Insufficient evidence that the rate has decreased.

Problem (Medium): The length, \(X\text{ mm}\), of components manufactured by an industrial process is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\text{ mm}\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\text{ mm}\). A quality assurance engineer tests the null hypothesis \(H_0: \mu = 20.0\) against the alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \mu > 20.0\) at the \(5\%\) significance level using an initial random sample of size \(n = 25\). The critical region for the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is found to be \(\bar{X} \ge 20.658\). Using the standard normal critical value \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\): 1. Find the value of \(\sigma\). 2. Hence, determine the minimum sample size, \(m\), required so that in a subsequent test of \(H_0: \mu = 20.0\) against \(H_1: \mu > 20.0\) at the same \(5\%\) significance level, the probability of committing a Type II error when the true mean is \(\mu = 21.0\) is at most \(0.05\).

Step-by-Step Solution: We solve the problem in two stages: **Step 1: Determine \(\sigma\)** Under \(H_0\), the distribution of the sample mean is \(\bar{X} \sim N\left(20.0, \frac{\sigma^2}{25}\right)\). The critical value for a upper one-tailed test at the \(5\%\) level corresponds to \(z = 1.645\): \[ \frac{20.658 - 20.0}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{25}}} = 1.645 \] \[ \frac{0.658}{\frac{\sigma}{5}} = 1.645 \implies \frac{3.29}{\sigma} = 1.645 \implies \sigma = \frac{3.29}{1.645} = 2.0\text{ mm} \] **Step 2: Determine the minimum sample size \(m\)** For a new sample of size \(m\), the rejection rule at the \(5\%\) level requires rejecting \(H_0\) if \(\bar{X} \ge c\), where: \[ c = 20.0 + 1.645 \left(\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}\right) = 20.0 + \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}} \] A Type II error occurs when \(H_0\) is not rejected (i.e. \(\bar{X} < c\)) given that the true mean is \(\mu = 21.0\). We require: \[ P(\bar{X} < c \mid \mu = 21.0) \le 0.05 \] Standardising under \(\mu = 21.0\): \[ \frac{c - 21.0}{\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}} \le -1.645 \implies c \le 21.0 - 1.645 \left(\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}\right) = 21.0 - \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}} \] Equating both conditions for \(c\): \[ 20.0 + \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}} \le 21.0 - \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}} \] \[ \frac{6.58}{\sqrt{m}} \le 1.0 \implies \sqrt{m} \ge 6.58 \] \[ m \ge 6.58^2 = 43.2964 \] Since \(m\) must be an integer, the minimum sample size is \(m = 44\). **Common traps:** - Rounding down to \(43\) yields a Type II error probability greater than \(0.05\). - Omitting the calculation of \(\sigma\) and erroneously assuming \(\sigma = 1\) yields \(m = 11\). - Omitting the critical value shift from one of the two tails leads to \(m = 22\).

Problem (Hard): A quality control protocol uses a two-stage hypothesis test to monitor the rate of flaws, \(\lambda\) per metre, in the production of high-grade optical fibre. The number of flaws in a length of fibre follows a Poisson distribution. The manufacturer tests: \[ H_0: \lambda = 1 \quad \text{against} \quad H_1: \lambda > 1. \] The two-stage procedure operates as follows: - **Stage 1:** A \(1\text{-metre}\) sample is inspected, and the number of flaws \(X_1\) is recorded. If \(X_1 \ge 3\), \(H_0\) is rejected immediately. If \(X_1 = 0\), \(H_0\) is accepted immediately. If \(X_1 \in \{1, 2\}\), the test proceeds to Stage 2. - **Stage 2:** A second, independent \(1\text{-metre}\) sample is inspected, and the number of flaws \(X_2\) is recorded. If \(X_1 + X_2 \ge 4\), \(H_0\) is rejected; otherwise, \(H_0\) is accepted. Given that the true flaw rate is \(\lambda = 2\) per metre, find the probability that a Type II error is committed.

Step-by-Step Solution: A Type II error occurs when \(H_0\) is accepted despite the true parameter value being \(\lambda = 2\) (i.e. \(H_1\) is true). Under \(\lambda = 2\), the independent counts \(X_1, X_2 \sim \mathrm{Po}(2)\). The probability mass function is: \[ P(X = k) = \frac{2^k \mathrm{e}^{-2}}{k!} \] Specifically: \[ P(X = 0) = \mathrm{e}^{-2}, \quad P(X = 1) = 2\mathrm{e}^{-2}, \quad P(X = 2) = 2\mathrm{e}^{-2} \] \(H_0\) can be accepted in two mutually exclusive ways: 1. **In Stage 1:** \(H_0\) is accepted immediately if \(X_1 = 0\): \[ P(\text{Accept in Stage 1}) = P(X_1 = 0) = \mathrm{e}^{-2} \] 2. **In Stage 2:** The test enters Stage 2 if \(X_1 \in \{1, 2\}\). \(H_0\) is then accepted if \(X_1 + X_2 \le 3\): - If \(X_1 = 1\), \(H_0\) is accepted if \(X_2 \le 2\): \[ P(X_2 \le 2) = P(X_2 = 0) + P(X_2 = 1) + P(X_2 = 2) = \mathrm{e}^{-2} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-2} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-2} = 5\mathrm{e}^{-2} \] \[ P(X_1 = 1 \cap X_2 \le 2) = (2\mathrm{e}^{-2})(5\mathrm{e}^{-2}) = 10\mathrm{e}^{-4} \] - If \(X_1 = 2\), \(H_0\) is accepted if \(X_2 \le 1\): \[ P(X_2 \le 1) = P(X_2 = 0) + P(X_2 = 1) = \mathrm{e}^{-2} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-2} = 3\mathrm{e}^{-2} \] \[ P(X_1 = 2 \cap X_2 \le 1) = (2\mathrm{e}^{-2})(3\mathrm{e}^{-2}) = 6\mathrm{e}^{-4} \] Combining these cases: \[ P(\text{Accept in Stage 2}) = 10\mathrm{e}^{-4} + 6\mathrm{e}^{-4} = 16\mathrm{e}^{-4} \] Therefore, the overall probability of a Type II error is: \[ P(\text{Type II error}) = \mathrm{e}^{-2} + 16\mathrm{e}^{-4} \approx 0.135335 + 0.293050 = 0.428385 \approx 0.428 \] **Common Misconceptions:** - Choice B (\(16\mathrm{e}^{-4}\)) accounts only for accepting \(H_0\) at Stage 2 and omits immediate acceptance at Stage 1 (\(X_1 = 0\)). - Choice C (\(4\mathrm{e}^{-2}\)) computes the conditional probability \(P(\text{Accept } H_0 \mid \text{Stage 2 is reached}) = \frac{16\mathrm{e}^{-4}}{4\mathrm{e}^{-2}} = 4\mathrm{e}^{-2}\) instead of the unconditional probability of a Type II error. - Choice D computes the probability of a Type I error under \(H_0\) (where \(\lambda = 1\)).

rows.en: Produces smaller or even negative variance for the difference of independent variables.
Always add variances of independent variables: \(\sigma_{X-Y}^2 = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2\).
Confuses the variance of the sample mean \(\sigma^2/n\) with its standard error.
Absence of sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\) is true.
Write in context: "There is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha\) level to reject \(H_0\)."

body.en: Exam Marking Tip (Cambridge International A Level (9709 Paper 3 / Paper 6)): Always state the distribution parameters explicitly (e.g., \(X \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) or \(\bar{X} \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\)) and sketch a quick shaded bell curve before standardizing to \(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\). This secures the method mark even if a rounding slip occurs later.

label.en: ⚠️ Cambridge 9709 Traps — One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Tests & Critical Values

body.en:
Deciding Tail Direction: The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) must be determined strictly from the context before looking at sample numbers. Neutral words like 'has changed' or 'is different' require a two-tailed test (\(H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0\)), splitting \(\alpha\) into \(\alpha/2\) in each tail (e.g. \(z = \pm 1.96\) at 5%). Directional words like 'has decreased' require a one-tailed test (\(z = -1.645\) at 5%).

Contextual Conclusion: Cambridge requires two parts in any hypothesis test conclusion: (1) A statistical decision: 'Reject \(H_0\)' or 'Do not reject \(H_0\)'. (2) An in-context non-assertive summary: 'There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to conclude that the mean weight has changed.' Never write 'proved that \(H_0\) is true'.

question.en:
A random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\text{Po}(\lambda)\). A single observation of \(X\) is taken to test \(H_0: \lambda = 6\) against \(H_1: \lambda < 6\) at the 5% level.
(a) Find the critical region.
(b) State the actual significance level.
(c) Find the probability of a Type II error if the true value of \(\lambda\) is 3.
question.ar:
A random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\text{Po}(\lambda)\). A single observation of \(X\) is taken to test \(H_0: \lambda = 6\) against \(H_1: \lambda < 6\) at the 5% level.
(a) أوجد critical region.
(b) State the actual signإذا كانicance level.
(c) أوجد احتمال a Type II error إذا كان the true value of \(\lambda\) is 3.

solution.en:
(a) Under \(H_0\), \(X \sim \text{Po}(6)\). Calculate cumulative probabilities:

\[P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248\]\[P(X \le 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735\]\[P(X \le 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197\]

Since \(P(X \le 1) < 0.05\) and \(P(X \le 2) > 0.05\), the critical region is \(X \le 1\) (i.e. \(X = 0\) or \(1\)).

(b) Actual significance level = \(P(X \le 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174\) (or 1.74%).

(c) Type II error occurs when we fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(\lambda = 3\). We fail to reject when \(X \ge 2\):

\[P(X \ge 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \le 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\text{ (3 s.f.)}\]
solution.ar:
(a) Under \(H_0\), \(X \sim \text{Po}(6)\). احسب cumulative probabilities:

\[P(X = 0) = e^{-6} \approx 0.00248\]\[P(X \le 1) = e^{-6}(1 + 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.01735\]\[P(X \le 2) = e^{-6}(1 + 6 + 18) = 25e^{-6} \approx 0.06197\]

Since \(P(X \le 1) < 0.05\) and \(P(X \le 2) > 0.05\), the critical region is \(X \le 1\) (i.e. \(X = 0\) or \(1\)).

(b) Actual signإذا كانicance level = \(P(X \le 1 \mid \lambda = 6) = 7e^{-6} \approx 0.0174\) (or 1.74%).

(c) Type II error occurs عندما we fail to reject \(H_0\) عندما \(\lambda = 3\). We fail to reject عندما \(X \ge 2\):

\[P(X \ge 2 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - P(X \le 1 \mid \lambda = 3) = 1 - e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 1 - 4e^{-3} \approx 1 - 0.1991 = 0.801\text{ (3 s.f.)}\]

question.en: [Practice 3 · Easy] A machine produces metal rods whose lengths are normally distributed with unknown mean \( \mu \text{ cm} \) and known standard deviation \( \sigma = 0.8\text{ cm} \). A quality control manager tests the hypotheses \[ H_0: \mu = 25.0 \quad \text{against} \quad H_1: \mu < 25.0 \] at the \( 5\% \) level of significance. A random sample of \( 16 \) rods yields a sample mean length of \( \bar{x} = 24.6\text{ cm} \). Given that the critical value for this test is \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \), which of the following gives the correct test statistic \( z \) and the corresponding conclusion?
question.ar: [Practice 3 · Easy] A machine produces metal rods whose lengths are normally distributed with unknown mean \( \mu \text{ cm} \) and known standard deviation \( \sigma = 0.8\text{ cm} \). A quality control manager tests the hypotheses \[ H_0: \mu = 25.0 \quad \text{against} \quad H_1: \mu < 25.0 \] at the \( 5\% \) level of signإذا كانicance. A random sample of \( 16 \) rods yields a sample mean length of \( \bar{x} = 24.6\text{ cm} \). إذا علمت أن the critical value for this test is \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \), which of the following gives the correct test statistic \( z \) and the corresponding conclusion?

hints.en: Under the null hypothesis \( H_0: \mu = 25.0 \), the sample mean \( \bar{X} \) of a random sample of size \( n = 16 \) from \( \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \) has standard error: \(\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{16}} = \frac{0.8}{4}\).
hints.ar: تلميح للحل: استخدم العلاقة \( H_0: \mu = 25.0 \) ، \( \bar{X} \) ، \( n = 16 \) ، \( \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \) ، \(\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{16}} = \frac{0.8}{4}\) لتبسيط الخطوة.

hints.en: Since this is a lower-tail test at the \( 5\% \) level with critical value \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \), the critical (rejection) region is \( z < -1.645 \).
hints.ar: تلميح للحل: استخدم العلاقة \( 5\% \) ، \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \) ، \( z < -1.645 \) لتبسيط الخطوة.

hints.en: Because \(z = -2.0 < -1.645\), the test statistic falls in the critical region. Therefore, we reject \(H_0\).
hints.ar: Because \(z = -2.0 < -1.645\), the test statistic falls in the critical region. وبالتالي، we reject \(H_0\).

solution.en:
1. Under the null hypothesis \( H_0: \mu = 25.0 \), the sample mean \( \bar{X} \) of a random sample of size \( n = 16 \) from \( \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \) has standard error:
\[ \sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{16}} = \frac{0.8}{4} = 0.2 \]

2. The standardized test statistic \( z \) is:
\[ z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{24.6 - 25.0}{0.2} = \frac{-0.4}{0.2} = -2.0 \]

3. Since this is a lower-tail test at the \( 5\% \) level with critical value \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \), the critical (rejection) region is \( z < -1.645 \).

4. Because \( z = -2.0 < -1.645 \), the test statistic falls in the critical region. Therefore, we reject \( H_0 \).

Common errors:
- Omitting \( \sqrt{n} \) gives \( z = \frac{24.6 - 25.0}{0.8} = -0.5 \), which leads to incorrectly failing to reject \( H_0 \).
- Dividing by \( n \) rather than \( \sqrt{n} \) gives \( z = \frac{-0.4}{0.8/16} = -8.0 \).
- Inverting the decision rule leads to falsely accepting \( H_0 \) despite the test statistic falling in the critical region.
solution.ar:
1. Under the null hypothesis \( H_0: \mu = 25.0 \), the sample mean \( \bar{X} \) of a random sample of size \( n = 16 \) from \( \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \) has standard error:
\[ \sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{16}} = \frac{0.8}{4} = 0.2 \]

2. The standardized test statistic \( z \) is:
\[ z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{24.6 - 25.0}{0.2} = \frac{-0.4}{0.2} = -2.0 \]

3. Since this is a lower-tail test at the \( 5\% \) level with critical value \( z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645 \), the critical (rejection) region is \( z < -1.645 \).

4. Because \( z = -2.0 < -1.645 \), the test statistic falls in the critical region. وبالتالي، we reject \( H_0 \).

Common errors:
- Omitting \( \sqrt{n} \) gives \( z = \frac{24.6 - 25.0}{0.8} = -0.5 \), which leads to incorrectly failing to reject \( H_0 \).
- Dividing by \( n \) rather than \( \sqrt{n} \) gives \( z = \frac{-0.4}{0.8/16} = -8.0 \).
- Inverting the decision rule leads to falsely accepting \( H_0 \) despite the test statistic falling in the critical region.

The length, \(X\text{ mm}\), of components manufactured by an industrial process is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\text{ mm}\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\text{ mm}\). A quality assurance engineer tests the null hypothesis \(H_0: \mu = 20.0\) against the alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \mu > 20.0\) at the \(5\%\) signإذا كانicance level using an initial random sample of size \(n = 25\).

The critical region for the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is found to be \(\bar{X} \ge 20.658\).

باستخدام standard normal critical value \(z_{0.05} = 1.645\):
1. أوجد قيمة \(\sigma\).
2. ومنه، حدّد minimum sample size, \(m\), required so that in a subsequent test of \(H_0: \mu = 20.0\) against \(H_1: \mu > 20.0\) at the same \(5\%\) signإذا كانicance level, the probability of committing a Type II error عندما the true mean is \(\mu = 21.0\) is at most \(0.05\).

solution.en:
We solve the problem in two stages:

**Step 1: Determine \(\sigma\)**
Under \(H_0\), the distribution of the sample mean is \(\bar{X} \sim N\left(20.0, \frac{\sigma^2}{25}\right)\).
The critical value for a upper one-tailed test at the \(5\%\) level corresponds to \(z = 1.645\):
\[
\frac{20.658 - 20.0}{\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{25}}} = 1.645
\]
\[
\frac{0.658}{\frac{\sigma}{5}} = 1.645 \implies \frac{3.29}{\sigma} = 1.645 \implies \sigma = \frac{3.29}{1.645} = 2.0\text{ mm}
\]

**Step 2: Determine the minimum sample size \(m\)**
For a new sample of size \(m\), the rejection rule at the \(5\%\) level requires rejecting \(H_0\) if \(\bar{X} \ge c\), where:
\[
c = 20.0 + 1.645 \left(\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}\right) = 20.0 + \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}}
\]
A Type II error occurs when \(H_0\) is not rejected (i.e. \(\bar{X} < c\)) given that the true mean is \(\mu = 21.0\).
We require:
\[
P(\bar{X} < c \mid \mu = 21.0) \le 0.05
\]
Standardising under \(\mu = 21.0\):
\[
\frac{c - 21.0}{\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}} \le -1.645 \implies c \le 21.0 - 1.645 \left(\frac{2.0}{\sqrt{m}}\right) = 21.0 - \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}}
\]
Equating both conditions for \(c\):
\[
20.0 + \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}} \le 21.0 - \frac{3.29}{\sqrt{m}}
\]
\[
\frac{6.58}{\sqrt{m}} \le 1.0 \implies \sqrt{m} \ge 6.58
\]
\[
m \ge 6.58^2 = 43.2964
\]
Since \(m\) must be an integer, the minimum sample size is \(m = 44\).

**Common traps:**
- Rounding down to \(43\) yields a Type II error probability greater than \(0.05\).
- Omitting the calculation of \(\sigma\) and erroneously assuming \(\sigma = 1\) yields \(m = 11\).
- Omitting the critical value shift from one of the two tails leads to \(m = 22\). [M1][A1]
